All timestamps are now anchored to the video itself, per shot, using each shot's frame-verified strike moment.
Your @58 shot now has its aim line. Tonight's session re-verified server-side: shot 3's line lies exactly along the stick, through the cue ball, stopping at the 4.
The jittery move-stop-move tail is fixed too (the overlay clock could step backwards between frames; it can't now).
Tonight's session is fully corrected; the rest of the library retrofits overnight.
This is phase 1 of the cleanup you called for. Phase 2 makes every shot go through ONE identical pipeline the moment it completes - no more some-shots-analyzed-some-not. Phase 3 is the UI redesign.

entries.title: Trails and aim lines stay glued to the right shot
entries.body:
You caught it exactly: during laggy loads, the overlay clock kept running from the previous position, so the previous shot's (perfectly drawn) trail animated over the wrong footage - and aim lines could show for a shot the picture hadn't reached yet. The player now refuses to draw any overlay while the picture can't match it, and every navigation resets the overlay clock.
Root cause 1: jumping between shots bypassed the overlay clock's reset, so during a slow seek it extrapolated from the old position - the old trail kept animating until the new shot's first frame arrived.
Root cause 2: in playlists that hop between session videos, a cached trail from the same shot NUMBER in the previous session could be reused. The cache now knows which session it belongs to.
New rule everywhere: mid-seek, mid-load, or mid-swap, the overlay layer goes blank instead of guessing - same philosophy as detection's 'show nothing rather than something wrong'.
An adversarial review of the whole overlay timing system also caught and fixed: stale scrub seeks replaying after navigation, the frame-scrubber serving another session's cached frames after a playlist hop, and background frame-warming making overlays flicker while paused.

entries.title: You were right: quick pop-ups go with misses
entries.body:
Overnight, every shot in the library (1,193 across 35 sessions) got its stroke measured. The pattern you predicted is real: 32% of your misses come with a stay-down under 1 second, versus 16% of your makes - exactly double. Your median hold is also 0.3s shorter on misses (1.27s vs 1.57s). Lifetime Stats now shows medians and quick-exit rates.
The averages almost hid this (1.58s vs 1.65s) - the signature is a fat tail of quick exits on misses, so the stats show median and %-under-1-second instead.
No shot in the library measured under 0.7s, so your 'pop-ups' are subtle - a 0.9s exit, not a jump. The camera catches what feels invisible.
Every shot's Details sheet now carries its own numbers - check a few of your misses against your makes.

entries.title: New metric: how long you stay down on the shot
entries.body:
Every shot now gets stroke measurements straight from the camera: how long your cue stays down after contact, your backstroke length, the pause at the top of it, and your practice-stroke count. Misses often come with popping up early - now there's a number for it, and Lifetime Stats compares your average stay-down on makes vs misses.
Verified frame-by-frame before shipping: 9 of 9 measured shots matched hand-checked ground truth within 0.1 seconds (a tenth shot, where the balls were moved by hand, correctly measured nothing).
The shot Details sheet shows a STROKE row: stay-down seconds, an early pop-up warning, pause milliseconds, backstroke length, practice strokes.
Under the hood the true strike moment is re-detected from the cue ball's disappearance (the tracker's shot clock runs ~2.4s late), and the cue stick is tracked even when your arm overlaps it.
These field names match your Bluetooth cue sensor's - when it's installed, both sources will measure the same things and check each other.

entries.title: Tracking sees through the grain now
entries.body:
Tonight's high-ISO footage was confusing the ball tracker (identity mix-ups ran 4x the usual rate). The analysis feed now gets cleaned of grain before the detector looks at it - measured on your grainiest session: fewer identity mix-ups, better ball numbering, and 12-13% more balls held per frame. Your recordings are untouched.
Verified on two separate 6-minute slices before enabling: identity hops down 15%, ball-number coverage up, track fragmentation down 14-21%, and more balls tracked per frame in both tests with no metric worse.
This is the software half of the grain fix. The camera half (1/250 shutter + half the ISO next time you're at the rig) removes grain at the source and roughly halves file sizes too.

entries.title: Trail animations keep up with the ball now
entries.body:
The animated trails lagged because the phone's browser reports video time slightly in the past, and three hidden per-frame costs were eating the iPhone's processing budget. The overlay now reads the exact time of each displayed frame, and those costs are gone.
The overlay clock now uses frame callbacks (exact presented-frame timestamps, iOS 15.4+) instead of the stale 'official playback position', with a clean fallback when paused or on older devices. This also fixes extra lag in Low Power Mode.
The frame cache that makes scrubbing instant was JPEG-encoding every single frame during playback; it now stores every 3rd frame (scrubbing still always hits, and the cache covers 70 seconds instead of 23).
Two canvas layers were being reallocated on every animation tick even when nothing was drawn - both now only rebuild when the size actually changes.

entries.title: Clips now start instantly on your phone
entries.body:
Every recording had its seek index at the wrong end of the file, so your phone had to download huge chunks (up to ~2 GB for a late shot in a long session) before it could play anything. The index now sits at the front: playing any shot needs ~5-10 MB. All 26 older recordings were fixed tonight, and every new recording fixes itself automatically.
The recorder writes 'fragmented' video on purpose - it means a crash can't destroy a recording mid-write. But fragmented files carry an empty index up front; iOS can't even learn the clip's duration from it, let alone jump to a shot, so Safari crawled the file from the beginning.
The fix re-containers the finished file (a pure copy, ~1.4 seconds per GB, no quality change) right after recording stops - before it ever reaches Dropbox. Crash safety is unchanged: the file stays fragmented while recording is live.
Also found: tonight's high-ISO settings inflate file bitrate 4.6x (16 Mbps vs 3.5), which multiplies every download. The grain recommendation coming separately addresses this too.

entries.title: You were right about the shutter — blur is fixed
entries.body:
The new camera settings are real and working: a crop of the fastest-moving thing in your latest clip (the cue stick mid-stroke) is tack sharp. My earlier claim that the shutter 'wasn't applying' was my measurement's fault — it was counting pieces of your cue stick as blurred balls.
The smear detector ranks elongated blobs, and a cue stick is naturally elongated — no motion needed. Once your 1/500 shutter made the balls crisp, stick fragments were the only stretched shapes left, and they topped the list looking like blur.
The decisive test: the fastest mover in session 18:55 (inter-frame extent 199px — full stroke speed) shows zero smear in a single frame. At the old 1/60 exposure it would have smeared ~75px.
What this unlocks: fast shots stop vanishing mid-flight. 39 of the 62 remaining uncategorized misses failed because the ball was never captured between strike and pocket — that failure class should not exist in new recordings.

entries.title: Fixed the laggy mouse and keyboard
entries.body:
The AI was hogging the graphics chip — the same chip Windows uses to draw your cursor and keystrokes, which is why typing felt broken whenever the app ran. Ball detection now runs on the CPU instead: your desktop got its graphics chip back (app's share: 69% → 0%), and detection barely slows down.
Root cause: DirectML inference saturated the Radeon 780M's 3D engine at ~30 inferences/sec. On an integrated GPU that's the exact engine the Windows compositor needs for the cursor, and GPU engines have no preemptive priority — which is why every process/thread priority fix failed to help.
Measured before choosing: CPU at 4 threads does a full tiled detection in 88ms (~11/sec) vs ~15/sec on the GPU. Detections verified identical between the two (6/6 balls matched within 2px, same numbers).
It's a setting (detection.inference_provider: auto/gpu/cpu), so a future camera-PC or GPU upgrade flips it back with one word. The CPU session is capped at 4 threads and the app runs below-normal priority, so your input always preempts it.

entries.title: 31 more misses solved — backlog down to 62
entries.body:
A smarter read of rattle-heavy shots (judging only the ball's initial run, not the chaos after it hits the jaws) solved 31 more misses. Trusted verdicts: 116 → 147. Uncategorized: 93 → 62.
A measurement pass showed most stuck shots weren't missing data — they were fully observed but their paths bend too much (rattles, rebounds) for a whole-journey fit. The verdict only ever needed the first straight run from contact, so that's what gets judged now, under an even stricter straightness bar.
Of the 62 remaining: 39 were never captured at all (the shutter-speed change will prevent these going forward), 21 are genuinely too messy to trust, 2 pointed at no pocket. All stay in your grading playlist rather than being guessed.
Your categorized misses now split about even left/right overall — with 'cut right, missed right' (overcut) still the single biggest bucket at 28.

entries.title: 77 backlog misses solved automatically
entries.body:
The forensic solver you pushed for went through the uncategorized pile: 77 of 171 misses now carry a verdict (Uncategorized 171 → 94, trusted verdicts 38 → 115). Your own corrections still outrank everything.
It re-opens only the blurry second of each miss and searches the narrow corridor physics allows, matched against that ball's own colour — about 8 minutes of compute for the whole pile, versus the 13-hour full rerun that measurably didn't work.
Interesting early signal: the newly solved misses split 36 left / 41 right — much more balanced than the first trusted batch suggested. Worth watching as the rest get graded.
Honestly held back: 54 shots where the fit wasn't trustworthy and 39 where the ball's flight was never captured at all — those stay in your grading queue rather than being guessed. 49 solved shots know the miss side but not the cut (the cue wasn't tracked); they're listed as 'cut unknown' and count toward totals.

entries.title: Miss verdicts now come from physics
entries.body:
Every clip's miss side is now read off a physics fit of the ball's whole path — the method that got both hand-verified shots right, including one the old approach called confidently wrong. Trusted misses grew 33 → 38 and the table updated.
The old approach judged direction from a few samples near the pocket, which a rattle could fool — your 4-ball shot and one other verified clip proved it. The new approach fits straight rolling legs to every observation of the ball and reads the verdict off the fit, with its own error bar deciding when to trust it.
Your grading queue (Uncategorized) still works exactly the same — and every verdict you enter keeps training the system's honesty checks.

entries.title: Tap a stats line to grade those clips
entries.body: Every miss subgenre in Lifetime Stats — including Uncategorized — is now a playlist. Tap it, watch the clips, and set Cut/Missed in each shot's Details. Grading an Uncategorized miss moves it into its subgenre and sharpens the table.
